--- title: "October 30 – November 1, 2026" date: 2026-10-30 description: "Network median 2.91 in (range 1.81–7.64 in); peak IVT 618 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ from the SSW; Vance within 1,500 km" categories: [IVT ≥ 250, Tropical cyclone nearby, Snow, Final] execute: freeze: auto --- ## Summary **How it came together.** In the last days of October a large dip in the jet stream (a trough) deepened over the eastern Pacific, anchored by a low off the Pacific Northwest. Southerly winds ahead of it began drawing subtropical moisture, along with leftover monsoon moisture, north out of Mexico on October 29. By October 30, NWS Flagstaff forecasters described a 20–30 knot low-level wind blowing straight up the Gulf of California, and air holding close to record moisture for the time of year. A smaller disturbance off Baja California was merging with the trough, which they expected to prolong the rain. A first, light round reached Flagstaff on the afternoon of October 30. The main surge came as the low dropped south toward northern California: early on November 1 the moisture organized into an atmospheric river stretching back to the tropics off western Mexico and aimed at northern Arizona. It arrived on ground already soaked by October's storms. **What fell.** Most of the rain fell between Saturday night, October 31, and Sunday evening, November 1, over about 19 hours. Rain gauges across Flagstaff caught a typical 2.91 inches, from 1.81 in at Flagstaff Landfill to 7.64 in at Waterline Rd #1 (Lenox-Wupatki Trails). The airport measured 3.96 in, about 25 times the normal for those 3 days. Only 2 Novembers since 1898 had a wetter 3 days. Snow fell only at the highest mountain sites; in town it was rain. Nights were mild for the season, about 12 °F above normal. **Why so much.** The atmospheric river drove the storm: 89% of the rain fell while it was overhead, and at its peak it carried about 2.5 times the moisture flow that defines one. **What it did.** By the morning of November 2, NWS Flagstaff reported 2 to 5 inches of rain, locally more, across and south of the Mogollon Rim, with some stream gauges above their record heights. The Little Colorado River at Winslow reached a record flood stage, and forecasters expected its levee to be overtopped within hours. Oak Creek near Cornville set a record of 27,200 cubic feet per second (cfs), topping 26,400 cfs in February 1980 (78 years of USGS measurements). Chevelon Fork near Winslow (22,500 cfs, behind January 1993), Chevelon Creek near Winslow (29,100 cfs, behind December 1978) and the Verde River near Camp Verde (111,000 cfs, behind February 1993) had their second-highest peaks on record. Closer to town, Newman Canyon above Upper Lake Mary ran at 5,570 cfs, about twice its previous record (10 years of measurements); Clay Ave Wash rose 5.5 ft, its highest since the sensor began in 2016; Sinclair Wash near University Heights rose 7.0 ft, its highest since the sensor began in 2019. (River flows are provisional.) ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Technical summary Across 37 gauges the event total ranged from 1.81 to 7.64 in (median 2.91 in). The central 80% of the network-mean rain fell between Oct 31 22:00 MST and Nov 1 17:00 MST (19 h). Moisture transport over Flagstaff reached atmospheric-river strength: ERA5 IVT was at or above 250 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ for 24 h and peaked at 618 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ from the SSW at Nov 1 05:00 MST. 89% of the network-mean rain fell while IVT was at or above 250. Vance came within 1,450 km of Flagstaff (Oct 29 17:00 MST, remnant disturbance). At the IVT peak, 500-hPa flow over Flagstaff was from the SW at 35 m s⁻¹, and the 500-hPa trough axis along 35.25°N was at 120.5°W, 804 km west of Flagstaff (5,593 m, against 5,724 m over Flagstaff). A closed 500-hPa low (5,517 m) was centred 1,032 km to the WNW, at 38.5°N 122.5°W. The strongest 250-hPa wind within 1,000 km was 60 m s⁻¹, 409 km to the WSW. The 250-hPa wind over Flagstaff peaked at 57 m s⁻¹ (Nov 1 11:00 MST), 6 h after the IVT peak. ::: ## Rain across the network ::: {#15df7151 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Event rain total at each city and county gauge (circle color and label show the total in inches; map cropped to the network) over shaded relief (USGS 3DEP), 200-m elevation contours, streams (USGS NHD) and highways (Census TIGER). Tap or click the map to open the frame full size.* ## What the forecasters said The National Weather Service office in Flagstaff discussed the moisture source in its Area Forecast Discussions as the event unfolded. Excerpts, quoted verbatim (links to the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive): - **Oct 29, 9:36 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610291636)): "A deepening long-wave trough over much of the eastern Pacific will begin to draw sub-tropical moisture and remnant Monsoonal moisture northward by tonight. … By late Saturday evening, a significant tropical moisture plume originating around 24N will take aim at Arizona, as the now fully developed west coast trough starts to move inland." - **Oct 29, 10:19 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610300519)): "A shortwave over the Pacific will move northeastward across Arizona, drawing northward some deep moisture with precipitable water values close to the 99th percentile for late October." - **Oct 30, 10:07 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202610301707)): "Moisture transport is underway, featuring a 20-30kt low-level jet pointed straight up the Gulf of California and into the Lower Colorado River Valley. This advection is due to a deepening trough along most of the west coast, as well as sub-tropical jet and s/wv now located around 29N/120W. … This air mass will be near records as far as PW is concerned for this time of year and the phasing of the two systems will allow for an extended period of moderate to heavy rainfall." - **Nov 1, 4:29 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202611011129)): "A concerning hydrological threat will evolve across Northern Arizona over the next 24 hours with the arrival of an atmospheric river. … Hydrological issues will be enhanced due to the already very saturated soil conditions, and it will take less rainfall than usual to cause problems." - **Nov 2, 10:08 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202611021708)): "Rain gauge and radar data suggest a widespread area 2 to 5 inches of rain (locally higher) has fallen since yesterday across and south of the Mogollon Rim, with some stream gauges exceeding record stage heights. … A record flood stage has been observed early this morning on the Little Colorado at Winslow, with the levee expected to be overtopped within the next several hours." ## Climate context - **Airport precipitation:** 3.96 in over 3 local days, against a 1991–2020 normal of 0.16 in for those days (25× normal). - **Rank:** the 3rd largest 3-day airport total in November among 129 years with data since 1898 (each year's largest 3-day total ending in November). - **Airport temperature:** highs averaged -7.3 °F and lows +12.3 °F relative to normal. - **Water year to date** (Oct 1, 2026 – Nov 1, 2026): airport 9.65 in (normal 1.57 in);
